summary: L-Alanyl-L-glutamine is a stable, highly soluble dipeptide used as an additive to parenteral (IV) nutrition to supply glutamine to patients who require nutritional support, such as critically ill or post-surgical patients. Free glutamine is unstable in solution, so the dipeptide form delivers it safely; it is hydrolysed in vivo to alanine and glutamine. It is given only as part of a complete parenteral nutrition regimen and is not FDA-approved.
indications: Supplementation of glutamine as part of parenteral nutrition in patients in catabolic or hypermetabolic states (e.g. critically ill, major surgery) who require intravenous nutrition

dosage.n: Should not exceed ~20% of total amino acid intake; add to PN bag

dosage.d: Up to 0.1 g amino acids/kg/hour from the dipeptide
dosage.n: Mix with a compatible carrier amino acid/PN solution

admin: Administer only as an additive to a carrier amino acid or parenteral nutrition solution - never alone as a separate infusion
Infuse intravenously, usually via central line, at controlled rate
Ensure the dipeptide does not exceed about 20% of total amino acid supply
Use aseptic technique; inspect for clarity before use
moa: After intravenous infusion, the dipeptide L-alanyl-L-glutamine is rapidly hydrolysed by ubiquitous peptidases into free L-alanine and L-glutamine. Glutamine is a conditionally essential amino acid and major fuel for rapidly dividing cells (enterocytes, immune cells); supplementation supports protein synthesis, gut integrity, antioxidant (glutathione) production, and nitrogen balance in catabolic states. The dipeptide form overcomes the instability and low solubility of free glutamine in solution.

absolute: Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below ~25 mL/min)
Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism
relative: Critically ill multi-organ failure (use cautiously given mixed trial evidence)

preg: Limited data in pregnancy. Use only when nutritional support is clearly required and under specialist supervision, weighing maternal benefit against uncertain fetal risk.
lact: Limited data during breastfeeding. Use only if clearly necessary and under specialist supervision.
renal: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl <25 mL/min) due to risk of accumulation and metabolic disturbance. Use cautiously with monitoring in lesser degrees of impairment.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic insufficiency. In lesser impairment, monitor liver function and ammonia, as impaired metabolism may cause accumulation.

moderate: Other components of parenteral nutrition (ensure overall amino acid/nitrogen balance)
minor: No clinically significant direct drug interactions reported
interactions.diagnostics: May transiently affect serum ammonia and amino acid panels

common: Generally well tolerated when infused correctly
Chills or transient infusion-related symptoms if infused too fast
serious: Metabolic disturbances (acid-base, ammonia accumulation) with organ impairment
emergency: Severe metabolic acidosis or hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in unsuitable patients

counsel: This is given through a drip as part of your IV nutrition while in hospital
Tell staff about any flushing, chills, or discomfort during the infusion
It supplies glutamine, an amino acid your body needs more of when seriously ill
Blood tests will monitor your liver, kidneys, and salts during treatment
pk: Rapidly hydrolysed to free amino acids within minutes of infusion
Plasma dipeptide peaks during infusion; quickly cleared
Very short dipeptide half-life (a few minutes); released amino acids enter normal pools
Effect tied to continuous infusion as part of parenteral nutrition
Store at room temperature (do not refrigerate/freeze); use immediately after admixture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; widely used in Europe/Asia (e.g. Dipeptiven) and supported by EMA/SmPC and ESPEN guidance rather than a US FDA label
The dipeptide form solves the instability and poor solubility of free glutamine in IV solutions
Always an additive to carrier amino acid/PN - never infused alone
Contraindicated in severe renal or hepatic failure
Clinical-outcome evidence in critical illness is mixed; routine high-dose use in multi-organ failure is discouraged by some guidelines
missed: Not applicable - administered as a continuous hospital infusion managed by clinical staff as part of parenteral nutrition.
overdose: Excessive or too-rapid infusion may cause metabolic disturbances such as acidosis, raised ammonia, chills, or nausea. Slow or stop the infusion and provide supportive care with monitoring of acid-base balance, ammonia, and renal/hepatic function.
